Abstract
               
                  Objective
                  Parents routinely access young children’s medical records, but medical societies strongly recommend confidential care during adolescence, and most medical centers restrict parental records access during the teen years. We sought to assess public opinion about adolescent medical privacy.
               
               
                  Materials and Methods
                  The Cornell National Social Survey (CNSS) is an annual nationwide public opinion survey. We added questions about a) whether parents should be able to see their 16-year-old child’s medical record, and b) whether teens would avoid discussing sensitive issues (sex, alcohol) with doctors if parents could see the record. Hypothesizing that highlighting the rationale for adolescent privacy would change opinions, we conducted an experiment by randomizing question order.
               
               
                  Results
                  Most respondents (83.0%) believed that an adolescent would be less likely to discuss sensitive issues with doctors with parental medical record access; responses did not differ by question order (P = .29). Most also believed that parents should have access to teens’ records, but support for parental access fell from 77% to 69% among those asked the teen withholding question first (P = .01).
               
               
                  Conclusions
                  Although medical societies recommend confidential care for adolescents, public opinion is largely in favor of parental access. A brief “nudge,” asking whether parental access might harm adolescent–doctor communication, increased acceptance of adolescent confidentiality, and could be part of a strategy to prepare parents for electronic patient portal policies that medical centers impose at the beginning of adolescence.

Abstract

Objective
Parents commonly view young children’s medical records, but medical organizations strongly advise confidential care during adolescence, and most medical centers limit parental access to records in the teen years. We aimed to evaluate public opinion on adolescent medical privacy.

Materials and Methods
The Cornell National Social Survey (CNSS) is an annual nationwide public opinion poll. We added questions asking a) whether parents should be permitted to see their 16-year-old child’s medical record, and b) whether teens would be less likely to discuss sensitive topics (sex, alcohol) with doctors if parents could view the record. To test the hypothesis that emphasizing the reason for adolescent privacy would affect opinions, we randomized the question order in an experiment.

Results
Most respondents (83.0%) thought an adolescent would be less likely to discuss sensitive issues with doctors if parents had access to the medical record; answers did not vary by question order (P = .29). Most also thought parents should have access to teens’ records, but support for parental access dropped from 77% to 69% among those asked the teen-withholding question first (P = .01).

Conclusions
Although medical societies recommend confidential care for adolescents, public opinion generally favors parental access. A brief “nudge” asking whether parental access could harm adolescent–doctor communication increased acceptance of adolescent confidentiality and may help prepare parents for electronic patient portal policies that medical centers introduce at the start of adolescence.
